Microaeration promotes volatile siloxanes conversion to methane and 
simpler monomeric products

H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Siloxanes can be converted to methane 
under anaerobic/microaerobic conditions. 
• Microaeration improves the kinetics of 
siloxane conversion to methane. 
• Microaeration modifies the ecological 
structure of the anaerobic microbiome. 
• Previous inoculum acclimatation is not 
required for siloxane biodegradation.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
Biogas 
Siloxane biodegradation 
Microbiome adaptation 
Emergent contaminants 
A B S T R A C T   
The ubiquitous use of volatile siloxanes in a myriad of product formulations has led to a widespread distribution of 
these persistent contaminants in both natural ecosystems and wastewater treatment plants. Microbial degradation 
under microaerobic conditions is a promising approach to mitigate D4 and D5 siloxanes while recovering energy in 
wastewater treatment plants. This study examined D4/D5 siloxanes biodegradation under both anaerobic and 
microaerobic conditions (PO2 = 0, 1, 3 %) using wastewater sludge. Results show that the use of microaeration in an 
otherwise strictly anaerobic environment significantly enhances siloxane conversion to methane. 16S rRNA gene 
sequencing identified potential degraders, including Clostridium lituseburense, Clostridium bifermentans and Syn­
ergistales species. Furthermore, chemical analysis suggested a stepwise siloxane conversion preceding methano­
genesis under microaerobic conditions. This study demonstrates the feasibility of microaerobic siloxane 
biodegradation, laying groundwork for scalable removal technologies in wastewater treatment plants, ultimately 
highlighting the importance of using bio-based approaches in tackling persistent pollutants.

1. Introduction 
Volatile siloxanes are used in many industrial and consumer prod­
ucts, particularly in pharmaceuticals and personal care products. In 
general, siloxane molecules are formed by two organosilane units, which 
are linked by a silicon-oxygen (Si–O) bond that can be arranged in 
oligomeric or polymeric forms (Wang et al., 2019). Polymeric siloxanes 
(e.g., polydimethylsiloxane, PDMS) are arranged as linear molecules 
with ten or more monomeric Si-O sub-units. Volatile siloxanes are ob­
tained from PDMS hydrolyzation via chemical synthesis, biochemical 
degradation (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 2021), or chemical rearrangement 
(Piechota and Buczkowski, 2014). Both forms are considered difficult 
biodegradation due to the high energy required to break their molecular 
bonds, particularly the Si–O bond in cyclic molecules, which is also 
shielded by the steric hindrance of Si-CH3 groups (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 
2023). This bond needs to be cleaved to open the siloxane ring, allowing 
the degradation of the molecule. 
Due to the industrially relevant characteristics of volatile siloxanes, 
these siloxanes have become almost irreplaceable in the formulation of a 
variety of industrial products (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 2023). As a result, 
there has been a considerable increase in their global production, 
reaching 10 million tons in 2020 (Mojsiewicz-Pie´nkowska and Krencz­
kowska, 2018). However, growth in volatile siloxane production has 
intensified their negative atmospheric impacts because they are pro­
duced faster than they are degraded naturally (Mojsiewicz-Pie´nkowska 
and Krenczkowska, 2018). Among the volatile siloxanes, octamethyl- 
cyclotetrasiloxane (D4) and decamethyl-cyclopentasiloxane (D5) are 
particularly important due to their prevalence in personal care products. 
D4 and D5 are recognized as emerging contaminants and substances of 
very high concern by the Evaluation, Authorization, and Restriction of 
Chemicals regulatory authority in the EU (European Chemical Agency, 
2018a,b), following similar regulatory policies in other countries. 
D4 and D5 siloxanes are washed down the drain and transported to 
wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) – making these facilities the 
primary concentration points of volatile siloxanes. Due to their high 
hydrophobicity, most of the volatile siloxanes concentrate in the 
wastewater secondary sludge. During anaerobic digestion, the D4 and 
D5 siloxanes contained in the sludge cannot be fully biodegraded, 
resulting in their release into the biogas. Upon combustion, the volatile 
siloxanes contained in the biogas cause irreversible damage to the 
equipment and a significant impact on the capital costs of the WWTP 
(Struk et al., 2020). WWTPs address these issues using physicochemical 
methods (e.g., activated carbon adsorption) to clean the biogas (Ortiz- 
Ardila et al., 2023). However, these methods, although effective at 
removing the siloxanes, only transfer these compounds to another me­
dium (e.g., biogas to sorbent matrix), requiring further treatment steps 
before disposal. 
To prevent the generation of waste by-products from D4 and D5 
biogas removal, their biological degradation has emerged as an alter­
native (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 2023). However, still there is no clear scien­
tific evidence on how microbes can overcome the steric hindrance in the 
D4 and D5 molecules (Wang et al., 2019). Furthermore, there is limited 
knowledge regarding the microbial conversion of D4 and D5 siloxanes 
into methane. Previous studies have demonstrated that D4 and D5 can 
be biologically converted to non-volatile final products (i.e., dime­
thylsilanediol, silanes) under aerobic conditions (Gaj, 2020). However, 
aerobic treatment systems require permanent air injection and yield up 
to 12 times more biosolids than anaerobic ones, resulting in high 
operating costs (van Lier et al., 2023). Nonetheless, anaerobic conditions 
alone are not sufficient to completely biodegrade D4 and D5 siloxanes 
due to the lack of a strong electron acceptor (e.g., oxygen) (Zhang et al., 
2020). 
The controlled addition of oxygen in an otherwise strictly anaerobic 
environment, known as microaeration, has the thermodynamic benefits 
of aerobic systems (i.e., stronger electron acceptor) while preserving the 
ecological relationships in the anaerobic microbiome (Wu et al., 2021). 
Indeed, previous studies have shown that anaerobic microbiomes can 
adapt to use oxygen, increasing the metabolic diversity and improving 
the biodegradation of recalcitrant pollutants (Duarte et al., 2018). 
However, studies on the use of microaeration for siloxane biodegrada­
tion are just emerging. A previous study assessing the biodegradation of 
D4 suggested that microaeration did not yield considerable changes in 
the microbiome ecology or a better reactor performance (Santos-Clotas 
et al., 2020). However, a recent study showed that PDMS were biode­
gradable and could be transformed into methane under microaerobic 
conditions once the microbiome acclimated and used oxygen (Ortiz- 
Ardila et al., 2021). 
Previous studies on aerobic D4 siloxane degradation highlight the 
role of oxygen in overcoming steric hindrance. But do these mechanisms 
apply under microaerated conditions? Can microbes convert volatile 
siloxanes into methane? Addressing these questions is crucial for 
assessing D4 and D5 siloxane microbial conversion feasibility and 
environmental impact. This study investigates microaeration effects on 
D4 and D5 biodegradation and methane conversion. Ecological shifts in 
anaerobic microbiomes under microaeration and siloxane supplemen­
tation were characterized, a theoretical reaction pathway for D4 ring 
opening was proposed, and the hypothesis that both siloxanes and 
microaeration reshape anaerobic microbiomes to effectively degrade 
and convert D4 and D5 into methane was tested. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Experimental design 
Biochemical methane potential (BMP) assays were used to assess the 
biological conversion of D4 and D5 siloxanes to methane under anaer­
obic and microaerobic conditions. BMPs were performed based on a 
randomized, full-factorial experimental design testing the following 
factors: 1) oxygen partial pressure (PO2); 2) inoculum type; and 3) D4:D5 
concentration. The experimental design includes combinations of all the 
tested factors with triplicates for each combination, with methane pro­
duction selected as the response variable. Further information about the 
experimental approach is provided in the supplementary information 
section (See supplementary material Table 1). For factor one, pure 
oxygen was supplemented at target partial pressures (PO2) of 1 % and 3 
% O2 for the microaerated treatments, while anaerobic conditions (PO2 
= 0 % O2) were used as a baseline control. For factor two, a fresh, non- 
acclimated inoculum from an anaerobic digester treating secondary 
sludge from a municipal wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) (La far­
fana, Santiago, Chile) was compared to an inoculum from the same 
digester following acclimation to microaerated conditions and a 
siloxane-type compound. This inoculum was acclimated to microaerated 
conditions (PO2 = 1 % O2) and fed a substrate mixture containing 50 
ppm of PDMS for six months prior to the BMP assays. For factor three, D4 
and D5 siloxanes (Technical grade – Sigma Aldrich) were supplemented 
in a 1:1 M ratio at a total concentration of 100 ppm (50 ppm of each 
molecule) and 1000 ppm (500 ppm of each molecule) in the feed 
mixture. The feed mixture contained glucose, sodium acetate, sodium 
casein, cellulose, and coconut oil in equal parts, on a chemical oxygen 
demand (COD) basis as described by Ortiz-Ardila et al. (Ortiz-Ardila 
et al., 2021). D4 and D5 siloxanes were cooled to 10 ◦C to reduce their 
volatility before application to the BMP bottle. Once the D4:D5 mix was 
dosed, the bottles were gently vortexed to facilitate the transfer of si­
loxanes to the organic matter (i.e., inocula) inside the bottle. 
Finally, four treatments were used as controls and comparisons for 
each of the experimental combinations: 1) an inoculum without any 
substrate, to account for endogenous methane production; 2) an inoc­
ulum with organic substrate and no-addition of D4:D5, to account for 
the anaerobic methane production of the organic substrate; 3) same as 
treatment 2) but under low microaeration, PO2 = 1 % O2, to account for 
the effect of oxygen addition in the conversion of organic substrate into 
methane; and 4) same as treatment 3) but with high microaeration, PO2

2.2. Biochemical methane potential (BMP) assay 
The BMP assay was based on Ortiz-Ardila et al. (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 
2021), using 250 mL Schott bottles at an inoculum-to-substrate ratio of 
2:1 (COD basis). Each experimental bottle included the D4:D5 mixture, 
the organic substrate, and a micronutrient solution (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 
2021). Once the bottles were filled, oxygen was removed from the 
headspace using a flow of nitrogen gas and then placed in a shaking 
incubator (90 rpm, 37 ± 1 ◦C). Twelve days into incubation, pure oxy­
gen (99.8 %) was added to each bottle by internal volume substitution 
with gas-tight syringes to reach the target oxygen partial pressure of 1 % 
and 3 % v/v. Subsequently, oxygen was added to each bottle on biogas 
measurement days to maintain the target O2 partial pressures. Finally, 
the volumetric biogas production was measured from each bottle using 
the volume displacement method (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 2021). The 
methane that was produced in the acclimated and non-acclimated 
inoculum bottles without any substrate was deducted from the 
methane production on each corresponding experimental bottle. The 
BMP assay was terminated when the cumulative biomethane production 
curve reached a plateau phase (ca. 55 days). 
2.3. Analytical methods 
The biogas composition (i.e., O2, CH4, CO2, N2) was measured using 
an Agilent 7820A gas chromatograph (GC) (Santa Clara, CA, USA) 
equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a Carbosphere 
1010 capillary column (Supelco-Merck, Germany), according to ASTM 
method D3612 (American Public Health Association et al., 2017). The 
lipophilic fraction of siloxanes was recovered from the post-digestion 
anaerobic sludge by solvent-assisted extraction using an n-hex­
ane–acetone mixture (1:1 v/v). Also, a tetrahydrofuran extract was ob­

The chemical structure of the extracted compounds was identified 
using a Shimadzu 8050 gas chromatography-mass spectrometer triple 
quadrupole (GC–MS-QQQ) (Kyoto, Japan). Samples with non-polar 
compounds, which were both derivatized and underivatized, were 
injected in splitless mode and separated with a capillary column (HP- 
5MS, 60 m × 0.25 mm x 0.25 µm, Agilent) with helium as a carrier gas at 
1 mL min−1, according to Sanchís et al. (Sanchís et al., 2013). The same 
samples were further analyzed for polar compounds using an Agilent 
HP-Innowax column (60 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 µm) based on the meth­
odology reported by Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2020). Selected ion 
monitoring (SIM) was used to detect siloxane-like compounds, which 
were later identified by cross-referencing the NIST14.L mass-spectra 
library at a 95 % similarity cut-off. 
2.4. Theoretical calculations, methane production modeling, and 
statistical methods employed 
The theoretical methane production of each substrate was estimated 
using the Buswell Formula (Bu) (Symons and Buswell, 1933), which is 
based on their molecular formula. For D4 and D5, the molecular 
formulae C8H24O4Si4 and C10H30O5Si5 were assumed. A Gompertz- 
Zwietering (GZ) model was implemented to assess the kinetic parame­
ters of methane production (i.e., lag phase duration, ultimate methane 
production, and absolute production rate) for the anaerobic and 
microaerated conditions (Tjørve and Tjørve, 2017). Model fit was 
assessed using Akaike’s information criterion to reduce model 
complexity and ensure goodness-f-fit and precision, according to 
Bonakdari & Zeynoddin (Bonakdari and Zeynoddin, 2022). Average 
volumetric methane production per treatment was fitted to the GZ 
model (Eq. (1) using non-linear least squares analysis in the stats 
package for R (R Core Team, 2021).

2.5. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and taxonomic classification 
The 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed to evaluate the 
change in microbial community composition before and after the BMP 
assay. DNA extraction was performed using the FastDNA™ Spin Kit for 
soil. 16S rRNA gene amplification was accomplished by PCR using 515F 
and 806R bacterial universal primers with Illumina overhang sequences 
for the MiSeq sequencing platform. As microaerated conditions espe­
cially modify the bacterial composition of the AD microbiome, these 
primers were selected to focus more on bacterial diversity instead of 
archaeal diversity, according to Hathaway et al. (Hathaway et al., 2021). 
PCR products were cleaned using Mag-Bind PCR Cleanup until a clear, 
unique band was detected by 1 % agarose electrophoresis. The MiSeq 
Illumina library was prepared using barcoded indexes Nextera XT Index 
kit V2 (Illumina Inc. California – US), following manufacturer in­
structions for dual indexing. 
Genomic library products were spectrophotometrically quantified 
using dsDNA Qubit (Thermo Inc., Waltham, MA, USA), standardized at 
4 nM concentration, and pooled for the MiSeq Illumina platform. 
Sequencing was carried out using the MiSeq Reagent Kit v2 (300 cycles) 
at the Max Planck Institute for Biology, Tübingen, Germany. 16S rRNA 
gene amplicon sequences were processed via Quantitative Insights Into 
Microbial Ecology 2 (QIIME2) (Bolyen et al., 2019). Sequences were 
demultiplexed using the QIIME2 default pipeline. Quality filtering, 
sequence joining, chimera removal, and general denoising were per­
formed using the Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm (DADA2). 
The obtained representative sequences were filtered by removing 
singletons and low-frequency sequences. Next, the filtered sequences 
were taxonomically classified using the machine-learning Scikit-learn I- 
Bayes custom-trained classifier. After an initial screening and compari­
son of the taxonomic classification of the 16S rRNA gene between the 
SILVA_138 and Greengenes 13_8 databases, the Greengenes database 
was chosen to train the I-Bayes classifier using the sequence of selected 
primers (i.e., 515F – 806R). This decision was based on its demonstration 
of fewer unassigned OTUs and classification results similar to those of 
the SILVA_138 database. The I-Bayes classifier was then trained, with a 
cut-off match identity set at 96 % acceptance, using the filtered repre­
sentative sequences to ensure classification accuracy to at least the 
taxonomic order level. Finally, unassigned operative taxonomic units 
(OTUs) were discarded (4 % of initial sequences) to perform α and β 
diversity analyses. 
2.6. Microbial ecology assessment 
The α diversity and β diversity metrics were used to evaluate the 
effect of each experimental treatment on microbial ecology. The α

pipeline with Shannon, Simpson, and dominance indices. In addition, 
a comparative heatmap was created to assess microbial composition in 
all the experimental conditions. This heatmap was created using the 
previously filtered sequences and taxonomic classification on the 
Ampvis2 package (Andersen et al., 2018) under an R-studio environ­

environmental conditions as eigenvectors. Also, a K-means cluster

acclimated) as a clustering parameter for the calculated Bray-Curtis 
diversity by the Stats package for R (R Core Team, 2021). Then, using 
a direct gradient analysis (DGA), significant microbes were ordinated 
with the constraints of the dbRDA analysis. dbRDA, DGA, clustering 
calculations, and plots were performed with the Vegan community 
ecology package for R. The raw fastq files were deposited at the National 
Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database (Accession 
number: PRJNA1089110). 
3. Results 
3.1. D4 and D5 siloxanes are biodegradable and can be converted to 
methane under anaerobic conditions even without biomass acclimation 
Volatile siloxanes (i.e., D4 and D5) were biodegraded and partially 
converted into methane under all the tested conditions. The theoretical 
methane yield of the organic substrate mixture is 39 mL CH4. The final 
methane yields in all 500 ppm D4:D5 treatments consistently exceeded 
the 39 mL CH4 under anaerobic and microaerated conditions (Fig. 1), 
suggesting that D4, D5, or both were biodegraded to some extent, even 
though D4 and D5 concentrations were not directly measured during the 
BMP assay. Likewise, a noticeable improvement in methane production 
was observed in the 50 ppm D4:D5 treatments compared with the 0 ppm 
D4:D5 controls under anaerobic conditions (Fig. 1 [A0 and B0]). 
Also, treatments with 500 ppm D4:D5 produced 36 % more methane 
than the control (i.e., no D4:D5 addition) (Fig. 1 [A0]). Similarly, using 
the acclimated inoculum under the same conditions yielded 60 % more 
methane than the control (Fig. 1 [B0]). However, there were no signif­
icant differences in the final methane yield between non-acclimated and 
acclimated inoculum treatments under anaerobic conditions (p 0.203; C. 
I.: 95 %) (Fig. 1 [A0 vs. B0]). These results show that biodegradation of 
D4 or D5 to siloxane-type compounds is possible without prior accli­
mation. Indeed, previous studies have shown that the biodegradation of 
D4 and D5 yields silanols and silanes under anaerobic conditions (San­
tos-Clotas et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014); however, the mechanisms of 
converting volatile siloxane into methane have not been elucidated. 
The anaerobic treatments using the acclimated inoculum showed 
increased methane production kinetics, but no effect was observed on 
the final methane yield. The Gompertz-Zwietering model predicted 
shorter lag times (Tlag) in the acclimated treatments vs. the non- 
acclimated ones (Table 1). However, non-acclimated treatments 
showed faster absolute methane production rates (Kz) than acclimated 
inoculum treatments. This outcome suggests that while acclimated 
inoculum treatments started methane production earlier, once the lag 
phase was over, the non-acclimated inoculum treatments were able to 
convert the substrate mixture more efficiently under anaerobic condi­
tions (Fig. 1 [A0 vs. B0]). These differences and the possible adaptative 
advantage of the non-acclimated inoculum can be related to the differ­
ential ecological composition of both inocula. 
The 16S rRNA sequencing results show that the inocula had different 
compositions in key microbes, which other studies have correlated to 
recalcitrant compound biodegradation. For example, the abundance of 
Clostridium bifermentans in the non-acclimated inoculum treatments 
was higher than in the ones using the acclimated inoculum (Fig. 2 [B]). 
This microbe has been previously reported to degrade recalcitrant 
compounds such as: 1) azo dyes (i.e., red 3B-A, black 5, yellow 3G-P)

acclimated inoculum treatments. These microbes have been associated 
with the hydrolytic stages of secondary sludge anaerobic digestion 
(Militon et al., 2015), the source of the inoculum used in this study. The 
increased abundance of generalists (i.e., Peptostreptococcaceae spp. and 
Clostridiales) and specialist (i.e., C. bifermentans) populations in the 
non-acclimated inoculum treatments may explain the differences in lag 
phase time and methane production rates (Kz) with the acclimated 
inoculum treatments. Treatments using non-acclimated inoculum had 
slower lag phases as specialist populations typically grow slower than 
generalist ones (Xu et al., 2022). Once C. bifermentans reach higher 
abundances, they might interact with the generalist’s populations, 
increasing the hydrolysis of the supplemented substrate and explaining 
the higher methane production rate (Kz) on the non-acclimated inoc­
ulum treatments compared with the acclimated one. 
On the other hand, the microbial composition of treatments using 
acclimated inoculum showed a lower abundance of Peptos­
treptococcaceae spp. and Clostridiales hydrolytic populations (Fig. 2 
[B]). However, these microbiomes showed a slightly higher abundance 
of Tissierrella_Soehngenia spp., another generalist group, which has 
been associated with the hydrolytic stage of anaerobic digestion (Vas­
concelos et al., 2019). Furthermore, Clostridium lituseburense abun­
dance was especially high in the acclimated inoculum treatments 
compared to the non-acclimated ones. C. lituseburense is known to hy­
drolyze benzene- and p-toluenesulfonates that can be further converted 
into methane in the anaerobic digestion trophic web (Shcherbakova 
et al., 2015). It also has been related to oxytetracycline resistance and its 
biodegradation under anaerobic conditions (Akyol et al., 2016). The 
compound p-toluenesulfonate is a cyclic organic compound with similar 
steric hindrances as cyclic siloxanes (Kino et al., 2021); hence, C. litu­
seburense ability to rapidly overcome steric hindrances may have 
contributed to D4 and D5 degradation, explaining the shorter lag times 
of the acclimated inoculum treatments. 
In the microbial composition of the pre-BMP, there were notable 
differences in the Synergistales order between the non-acclimated and 
acclimated inocula (Fig. 2, and supplementary material Fig. S1). The

increased slightly with microaeration (Fig. 1). However, there were no 
significant differences in methane yields between the non-acclimated 
and acclimated inocula for either the 1 % or 3 % PO2 microaeration 
treatments (p-value: 0.538; C.I.: 95 %), indicating that microaeration, 
while advantageous, is not required for D4 or D5 biodegradation. 
Furthermore, high oxygen concentrations can slightly hinder methane 
production in non-acclimated treatments. For example, treatment T5_N 
(Fig. 1 [A2]) exhibited a lower methane yield compared to the control 
without D4:D5 supplementation. These results suggest that while 
microaeration may enhance the hydrolysis stages of anaerobic digestion 
(AD), there are still stochastic factors regarding how the microbiome 
reacts to high oxygen pressures (P0O2) that require further study and 
elucidation. 
Previous studies link the improved methane yields during microa­
eration to an oxygen-driven reshaping of the AD microbiome that en­
hances the hydrolytic stage (Montalvo et al., 2018). Oxygen is thought to 
increase the abundance of facultative anaerobes (e.g., heterotrophs), 
thereby increasing the metabolic diversity of the reactor microbiome 
(Nguyen et al., 2019). These facultative microbes quickly utilize the 
supplied oxygen, maintaining low oxygen and redox potentials to pro­
tect oxygen-sensitive microbes (e.g., acetogens and methanogens) 
(Nguyen et al., 2019). Here, Tissierrella Soehngenia spp. and Tepid­
imicrobium spp. were more abundant in the pre-BMP acclimated inoc­
ulum, suggesting microaeration favored clostridial populations (Fig. 2, 
and supplementary material Fig. S1). Clostridia populations produce 
potent lipases, proteases, and esterases, that make them particularly 
effective in hydrolyzing lipids, proteins, and carboxylic acids (Damodara 
Kannan et al., 2020). For example, methane production rates increased 
by 38 % and 44 % in the treatments with acclimated inoculum, 50 ppm 
D4:D5 supplementation, and 1 % PO2 and 3 % PO2, respectively 
(Table 1). The lag phase also decreased from 1 to 3 days compared to the 
anaerobic treatments. Previously, increased abundance of clostridia 
populations has been associated with siloxane biodegradation systems. 
Flores-Salgado et al. described a significant rise in Clostridium genus 
abundance within a two-stage system treating D4 and D5 siloxanes 
under anoxic conditions (Flores-Salgado et al., 2023). However, the 
volatile siloxanes biodegradation was attributed to Mycobacterium spe­
cies as the primary responsible for D4 and D5 removal. Thus, the higher 
diversity and abundance of Clostridia may have contributed to the 
observed increase in kinetics, methane yields, and D4:D5 metabolism 
through enhanced hydrolytic processes, rather than directly trans­
forming siloxanes molecules. 
However, for the 500 ppm D4:D5 treatment, microaeration did not 
significantly improve kinetics, which may have been caused by inhibi­
tion from D4:D5 metabolites. Previous reports showed siloxane catab­
olism produced antimicrobial metabolites (i.e., phenol, aliphatic 
alcohols) that inhibited methane production at high initial siloxane 
concentrations (e.g., 500 ppm) (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 2021). These inhib­
itory effects may be concentration-dependent and, thus, only manifest in 
batch systems. If hydrolysis rates increase due to microaeration, the 
conversion rates of subsequent trophic steps, such as acetogenesis and 
methanogenesis, must increase proportionally to prevent an accumula­
tion of intermediate products (Duarte et al., 2018). When microaeration 
was applied, the Synergistales order was more abundant in the accli­
mated treatments than the non-acclimated treatments (Fig. 2 [A vs. C vs. 
D]). When exposed to microaeration, HA73 Synergistales increased 
more than 60 % in abundance in the non-acclimated treatments but 
decreased by ~ 50 % in the acclimated treatments (Fig. 2 [A vs. C vs. 
D]). However, the inverse occurred for Aminobacterium spp. between 
treatments. In the non-acclimated inoculum, Aminobacterium spp. 
constituted less than 9 % of the community composition, whereas in the 
acclimated inoculum, they represented over 15 %. 
Previous reports correlated Synergistales abundance under stress 
conditions (e.g., ammonia, high organic loading rate (OLR)) with 
improved hydrolysis rates and methane production (Militon et al., 
2015). For example, Dur´an et al. (Dur´an et al., 2018) found that the 
abundance of Aminobacterium spp. significantly increased in an 
anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) when the system was oper­
ated at a high organic loading rates (OLR) resulting in higher hydrolysis 
rates and methane production. Also, in an anaerobic system treating 
tuna cooking wastewater, with high ammonia content, HA73 Synergis­
tales, which constituted 69 % relative abundance, were linked to 
peptone and amino acid degradation (Militon et al., 2015). HA73 Syn­
ergistales are syntrophic fermentative bacteria that have strong syn­
trophy with methanogenic archaea (Damodara Kannan et al., 2020), 
thus helping to maintain the balance between propionate, H2, and ace­
tate levels in anaerobic systems under stress (e.g., high OLR, high copper 
and sulphate concentrations) (Jordaan et al., 2019). These reports 
support the inferences on a microbial ecology re-balance when 
microaeration is applied for D4:D5 siloxanes conversion to methane. 
The distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA) shows a strong 
correlation between methane production, oxygen addition, acclimated 
inoculum, and the microbial community composition (Fig. 3). The 
abundance of key species such as C. bifermentans, C. lituseburense, and 
Rhodococcus spp. increased in response to microaeration in the non- 
acclimated and acclimated treatments (Fig. 2, and supplementary 
material Fig. S1). These microbial populations have been related to the 
biodegradation of recalcitrant compounds under anaerobic conditions 
(Shcherbakova et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2004), and some studies further 
suggest that microaeration can enhance their growth and metabolic 
capacities (Katarzyna et al., 2014). For example, the ability of C. bifer­
mentans to degrade recalcitrant compounds has been shown to increase 
under microaerated conditions (Katarzyna et al., 2014; Myszka et al., 
2012). Rather than intracellular adsorption, the degradation of complex 
molecules by C. bifermentans is mediated by extracellular enzymes with 
high redox capacity (Joe et al., 2008; Myszka et al., 2012). 
The degradation rate of recalcitrant compounds by C. bifermentans 
depends on enzyme concentration and activity. Accordingly, a higher 
cell count (i.e., abundance) yields higher amounts of these extracellular 
enzymes and, therefore, a higher activity. In this study, microaeration 
increased the abundance of C. bifermentans compared to anaerobic 
conditions in the non-acclimated treatments (Fig. 2 [B vs. C]). Myszka 
et al. (Myszka et al., 2012) suggested that C. bifermentans spores 
germinate faster in microaerated media than in anaerobic media, pro­
ducing more metabolically active vegetative cells. Finally, the dbRDA 
analysis shows a strong correlation between PO2, D4:D5 concentrations, 
and C. bifermentans abundance (Fig. 3), suggesting that these microbes 
may have played a role in D4:D5 degradation. 
C. lituseburense and Rhodococcus spp. also correlated with the D4: 
D5 conversion to methane (Fig. 3). The abundance of these microbes 
differed significantly between inocula treatments (Fig. 2 [B vs. C]). C. 
lituseburense abundance was > 5 % in all acclimated treatments and 
below detection limits in non-acclimated treatments (Fig. 2). In contrast, 
the abundance of Rhodococcus spp. was ~ 100 % higher in the accli­
mated treatments compared with non-acclimated ones (Fig. 2, and 
supplementary material Fig. S1). Rhodococcus spp. are known for 
their metabolic diversity, ecological adaptability (Kuyukina and Ivshina, 
2019), and their ability to degrade recalcitrant compounds under 
microaerobic conditions (Fuller et al., 2010), including PDMS (Ortiz- 
Ardila et al., 2021). Supporting these results, members of Rhodococcus 
genus have also been identified in biotrickling filters utilized for treating 
volatile siloxanes. Specifically, Rhodococcus sp., Rhodococcus erythrop­
olis, and Rhodococcus qingshengii were reported as part of a siloxane 
degradation community reported by Boada et al. (Boada et al., 2020) 
Rhodococci are thought to participate in the oxidative catalysis of (poly) 
aromatic compounds using dioxygenase enzymes (Fahy et al., 2008). 
Furthermore, the abundance and metabolic capabilities of Rhodococcus 
spp. have been shown to increase under low-oxygen concentrations

alcohols.

The D4 molecule mass-fragmentation pattern confirmed the attachment

peak was related to the Si-CH2-OH fraction in molecule 2, indicating that 
the D4 siloxane methyl substituents were oxidized (Fig. 4 molecule 2 – 
A). The results suggest that facultative anaerobes might remove the 
steric hindrance on siloxane molecules to allow their stepwise biodeg­
radation. Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2014) reported the same initial 
biodegradation process but under aerobic conditions, asserting that the 
oxidation of methyl groups in the siloxane molecule is only possible 
when a strong final electron acceptor (i.e., oxygen) is available. 
Once terminal alcohols replace the methyl groups (Fig. 4 molecule 
2), microbes can oxidize them to aldehydes (Fig. 4 molecule 3) and 
derive energy. Molecule 3 was identified by the mass peak at 324 Da and 
the mass fractions 57 m/z, 73 m/z, and 85 m/z, showing the oxidation from 
the Si-CH2-OH to the aldehyde substituent Si-CH-O. These stepwise re­
actions involving microbial metabolism have never been described for 
siloxane molecules. The reaction products suggest the presence of de­
hydrogenase enzymes that use the NAD+ aerobic system to catalyze 
alcohol oxidation. Subsequent reaction steps suggest a possible nucleo­
philic attack on the aldehydes carbonyl center that removes the carbonyl 
group and substitutes the –OH radical (Fig. 4 molecule 4). Molecule 4 
was identified by mass peaks 300 m/z, 298 m/z, and mass fraction 94 m/z, 
which confirm the Si-OH bond. The resultant alcohol attached to the Si 
atom is subject to electron repulsion between its terminal –OH free 
electrons and the oxygen free-electron pairs in the Si-O-Si cyclic struc­
ture. This repulsion and the availability of free electrons provide a target 
area for nucleophilic reactions on the Si-O-Si structure that opens the 
cyclic configuration. 
Previous D4 and D5 degradation studies report that once the siloxane 
ring is open, catalysis of the linear molecule proceeds stepwise (Accet­
tola et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2020), breaking the molecule down one 
monomer at a time (Li et al., 2014). The mass spectra results identified 
the cleavage product of the octamethyltetrasiloxanol molecule, sup­
porting this explanation (Fig. 4 molecule 5). Once the D4 molecule is 
open, the OH terminals become susceptible to further reactions with 
other compounds. For example, the isobutyl substituent in molecule 5 
(Fig. 4 molecule 5) might result from forming an ether bond between the 
linear siloxane molecule and the metabolite, isobutanol. Other studies 
support these inferences, showing that alkyl siloxanes or siloxane mol­
ecules with long organic substituents, such as molecule 5B, are more 
susceptible to biodegradation once other organic substituents are 
attached (Ro´sciszewski et al., 1998). 
On the other hand, trimethylsiloxane 5A, as a by-product, might be 
released after the Si-O bond is broken in molecule 5 and further cata­
lyzed by the demethylation of the isobutyl substituent (Fig. 4 molecule 
5A1). This reaction has been previously described in Rhodococcus sp. 
(Venkatesagowda and Dekker, 2021). Rhodococcus spp. performs iso­
butyl demethylation using oxygen-dependent demethylases that trans­
form alkyl products into simpler molecules that can be further 
metabolized (Venkatesagowda and Dekker, 2021). Other species have 
also been reported to perform demethylation reactions in anaerobic 
digestion microbiomes. For example, Boada et al. reported that Methyl­
ibium spp. use methylotrophic reactions to obtain energy from siloxanes 
for metabolism and growth (Boada et al., 2020). The elucidation of 
chemical reactions suggests D4 was similarly degraded to CO2 biologi­
cally through the oxidation of alkyl substituents (i.e., butyl, methyl, 
ethyl), which yielded energy for growth or metabolism. The identifica­
tion of methyl ether (molecule 5A2), which might be produced by the 
demethylation and oxidation of the by-product ethoxy(trimethyl)silane 
(5A1), supports this explanation. As previously reported, dimethoxy 
(dimethyl)silane (5A2) can be converted into dimethylsilanediol 
(DMSD) (Fig. 4 molecule 8) as one of the final products of D4 or D5 
biodegradation (Ortiz-Ardila et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). 
In addition, L3 siloxane molecules (Fig. 4 molecules 6A, 6B) that 
were not present at the beginning of the BMP assay, nor the controls 
without siloxanes, were identified in the post-BMP samples. The pres­
ence of L3 molecules indicates D4 or D5 was degraded. It is inferred that 
these L3 molecules were metabolized to DMSD by cleaving one siloxane 
monomer at a time, as suggested by Li et al. (Li et al., 2014). This 
metabolic process is mediated by oxidation reactions that convert the 
methyl substituents into Si-O-CH3 ethers, which are further transformed 
into methanol and CO2 (Li et al., 2014). The methanol and CO2 may 
have been used by methylotrophic and hydrogenotrophic methanogens, 
explaining the increased methane production in the BMP assays. The 
proposed pathway shares multiple similarities with the previously re­
ported D4 aerobic biodegradation pathway (Wang et al., 2014), sug­
gesting microaerobic conditions were bioenergetically sufficient to 
enable this pathway. The body of results presented here strongly sug­
gests volatile siloxanes can be biodegraded, and their by-products can be 
converted to methane in a methanogenic-microaerobic system, 
demonstrating that aerobic/anaerobic biochemical reactions can co- 
occur in a single reactor-developed microbiome. 
3.4. Microaeration as a practical strategy to reduce volatile siloxanes in 
anaerobic digestion 
Microaeration has been tested extensively at the lab scale since the 
2000 s to enhance organic matter biodegradability, methane produc­
tion, and hydrogen sulfide (H2S) removal (Chen et al., 2020). Initial 
reports showed a significant enhancement of over 40–60 % in methane 
production under microaerated conditions compared with anaerobic 
controls (Chen et al., 2020). Microaeration has been upscaled to ~ 200 L 
pilot- and ~ 400 m3 full-scale capacities using various bioreactor con­
figurations and substrates (e.g., primary sludge, wastewater, sewage 
sludge) (Nguyen et al., 2019). Microaeration is a well-known and robust 
strategy for removing H2S from biogas during anaerobic digestion while 
improving COD removal (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). Furthermore, 
multiple studies have explored using microaeration to shape anaerobic 
digestion microbiomes for improved performance (Chen et al., 2020; 
Menezes et al., 2019). 
Despite the considerable research and developmental effort around 
microaeration, full-scale applications outside biogas desulfurization are 
limited. The application of microaeration to biodegrade recalcitrant 
compounds is still in its early stages (Chen et al., 2020). This work and 
other laboratory-scale experiences show that microaeration can improve 
the biodegradation of recalcitrant or toxic compounds, such as siloxanes, 
phenols, furans, sulfonates, and azo dyes (Chen et al., 2020; Menezes 
et al., 2019). However, mechanistic explanations of how microaeration 
promotes the biodegradation of complex substrates, shapes the micro­
biome, and improves microbial kinetics are lacking and require further 
study. This work contributes to these explanations by demonstrating 
how microaerated conditions shape the microbiome to enable methane 
production from volatile siloxanes and by providing insights into the 
dynamics of D4 biodegradation. Furthermore, this study intends to 
provide an initial proof of concept to encourage other researchers to test 
and scale microaeration strategies for treating volatile siloxanes and 
other recalcitrant pollutants. 
4. Conclusions 
• D4:D5 were biodegraded and converted into methane under anaer­
obic conditions using acclimated and non-acclimated inocula.  
• Oxygen partial pressures of ~ 3 %PO2 improved biodegradation of 
D4:D5 and increased methane yields.  
• Microaeration reshaped the anaerobic microbiome, promoting 
facultative species enrichment and improving process kinetics.  
• D4 biodegradation under microaerated conditions likely involved a 
stepwise process that overcame the steric hindrances by first 
oxidizing the siloxane ring methyl groups.
